summary: A computer accepts input, processes it under a stored program, stores data and produces output: the IPO-S cycle. Its characteristics are speed, accuracy, diligence, versatility, storage, automation and reliability — with no IQ.
Five generations: vacuum tube → transistor → IC → microprocessor → AI/ULSI. Babbage is the Father of Computer; the Intel 4004 (1971) began generation four.
Speed units: Hz/MHz/GHz, MIPS, FLOPS; time units ms, μs, ns, ps with T = 1/f. Storage: 8 bits = 1 byte, and 1 KB = 2^10 bytes, each further step × 2^10.
Classification by power: supercomputer > mainframe > mini > microcomputer.
Architecture = what the machine does (programmer's view); organization = how it is built (implementation).
Block diagram: input → CPU (CU + ALU + registers) ↔ primary memory ↔ secondary storage → output, with control signals from the CU to every unit.
An n-bit address bus addresses 2^n locations; the address bus is unidirectional, the data bus bidirectional, the control bus carries commands.
RAM is volatile (SRAM = cache, DRAM = main memory); ROM is non-volatile (MROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash). Cache speeds repeat access; a buffer matches unequal speeds.

summary: A positional number in base r has value Σ di r^i. To decimal: expand positionally. From decimal: divide repeatedly (integers, read up) or multiply repeatedly (fractions, read down).
Binary ↔ octal groups 3 bits per digit; binary ↔ hex groups 4 bits. Octal ↔ hex must go through binary.
Binary addition: 1+1 = 10; subtraction borrows a 2.

1's complement = invert all bits, and the end-around carry is added back. 2's complement = 1's complement + 1, and the carry is discarded. No carry in either method means the answer is negative — recomplement and add a minus.
Boolean algebra (Boole 1854, applied by Shannon 1938) uses only 0 and 1, with + = OR, · = AND and a bar for NOT.
Seven gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR ("different"), XNOR ("same"). NAND and NOR are universal.
Half adder: S = Aoplus B, C = A· B. Full adder: S = Aoplus Boplus Cin, Cout = AB + (Aoplus B)Cin.
Key laws: A+A=1, AcdotA=0, A+AB=A, A+AB = A+B, A+BC = (A+B)(A+C), and De Morgan A+B = AB, AB = A+B.

summary: Software is the set of programs that tells hardware what to do. The syllabus categories are system, utility, application, web-based and mobile apps.
An operating system is the interface between user and hardware and the manager of all resources. Its functions are process, memory, file, device, security and user-interface management.

Multiprogramming: many jobs, one CPU, switch on I/O wait. Multitasking: many jobs, one CPU, switch on time slice. Multiprocessing: many CPUs in one machine, true parallelism. Distributed: many machines on a network acting as one.

Windows is a GUI (WIMP) operating system whose desktop, taskbar, Start menu, windows and File Explorer follow one consistent design. Know the parts of a window and the standard file operations and shortcuts.
A file path names a drive, the chain of folders and the file with its extension, for example D:\Class11\Computer\notes.docx.
Control Panel and Settings configure the system; system tools such as Disk Cleanup, Task Manager, Device Manager and System Restore maintain it.

Open source means the source code is published and may be modified. UNIX (Bell Labs, 1969) is the ancestor; Linux (Torvalds, 1991) is the free UNIX-like kernel, delivered as distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and Mint.
Mobile operating systems are touch-first, power-aware and sandboxed. Android (Linux based, open) and iOS (Apple, closed) together hold almost the whole market.

summary: An application package is ready-made software sold to many users; an office package bundles a word processor, spreadsheet, presentation tool and DBMS that share a common interface.
A word processor creates and formats text: editing, styles, tables, header and footer, spell check, mail merge. Examples: MS Word, LibreOffice Writer.

A spreadsheet holds data in cells addressed by column letter and row number, calculates with formulas beginning with = and functions such as SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, IF, and draws charts. References may be relative (B2), absolute (B2) or mixed.
Presentation software builds a deck of slides with layouts, themes, transitions and animations, shown with F5.
A DBMS stores data in tables of records made of fields, identified by a primary key and linked by a foreign key; its objects are tables, queries, forms and reports.

Domain-specific tools are built for one field: school management, inventory, payroll, financial accounting, hotel management and weather forecasting. Describe each by its inputs, processing and outputs.

summary: Languages run from 1GL machine code (binary, machine dependent, fastest) up through 2GL assembly (mnemonics, needs an assembler), 3GL high-level (C, Java — machine independent, needs a compiler or interpreter) to 4GL (SQL — you say what, not how).

A compiler translates the whole program at once and produces an executable; an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time and produces no file. Compiled code runs faster; interpreted code is easier to debug.

Syntax errors are caught by the compiler and stop it producing a program; semantic (logical) errors compile fine and give wrong answers; runtime errors such as divide-by-zero appear only while running.
The three control structures are sequence, selection (if, if-else, if-else-if, switch) and iteration (while, do-while, for). Every program can be built from these three alone.
Design tools: algorithm (numbered English steps), flowchart (oval = terminal, parallelogram = I/O, rectangle = process, diamond = decision), pseudocode (keywords plus English).

Absolute binary codes the whole number; BCD codes each decimal digit in 4 bits; ASCII codes characters in 7 bits (128 codes: A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48, space = 32); Unicode gives every character of every language its own code point and contains ASCII as its first 128 codes.
C was written by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972. It is a middle-level, structured, portable, case-sensitive language with 32 keywords. Every program has exactly one main().
C's six tokens are keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, operators and special symbols. An identifier starts with a letter or _, contains only letters, digits and _, and is not a keyword.

summary: The internet is the network; the World Wide Web is one service running on it. A browser is software on your device; a search engine is a website that indexes other sites using a crawler, an indexer and a ranking step.
The web uses the client–server model: DNS turns the name into an IP address, the browser sends an HTTP request, the server sends an HTTP response with the HTML.
A CMS (WordPress, Joomla, Drupal) stores content in a database and pours it into templates, so people can publish without writing HTML.
HTML structures a page, CSS presents it, JavaScript gives it behaviour. HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.

Every document has , , (with the compulsory ) and <body>. A tag names an element; an attribute (name="value") sits inside the opening tag and modifies it. <br>, <hr>, <img>, <meta>, <link> and <source> are empty tags.
Headings run <h1> (largest) to <h6>. <font size="1..7"> defaulted to 3. bgcolor, text, background, align, <font>, <basefont>, <big> and <bgsound> are all obsolete in HTML5 — CSS replaces them.

summary: Multimedia is the computer-controlled, integrated use of more than one medium — text, graphics, audio, video and animation — usually with interactivity.

Linear multimedia runs in a fixed order with no user control (a film); non-linear multimedia lets the user choose the path (a website, a game). Hypermedia is non-linear multimedia joined by hyperlinks.
Text is the smallest component and carries exact meaning; fonts are measured in points (1 point = 1/72 inch); formats .txt, .rtf, .docx, .pdf, .html.

Graphics are still pictures. Raster images are grids of pixels, are resolution dependent and go blocky when enlarged (JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP); vector images store shapes as mathematics, are resolution independent and stay sharp (SVG, AI, EPS, CDR).
Image size depends on resolution (pixels), colour depth (24-bit true colour = 16.7 million colours) and compression — lossy (JPEG) discards detail, lossless (PNG, GIF) does not.
Audio is digitised by sampling: CD quality is 44,100 Hz at 16 bits. MP3 is lossy and small, WAV is uncompressed and large, MIDI stores instructions rather than sound.
Video is captured frames plus synchronised sound, measured in frames per second (24 fps cinema, 25–30 fps television). A codec compresses it; a container (.mp4, .avi, .mkv) holds the parts together.
Animation is drawn or computed frames, not captured ones, and works by persistence of vision. Methods: frame-by-frame, tweening between key frames, path animation and morphing; 2D against 3D.
